newsitem.title: USA: Oregon boy, 12, on trial for killing 8 Mexicans.
newsitem.headline: Oregon boy, 12, on trial for killing 8 Mexicans.

text.p: A 12-year-old boy who started a fire that killed eight Mexican immigrants, including an entire family, should not be held responsible because of limited mental capacity, defense attorneys said on Wednesday.

In opening arguments on behalf of one of Oregon's youngest defendants, attorney Jennifer Harrington argued that Ray DeFord did not know what he was doing when he used newspapers to start the June 1996 apartment house fire in a Portland suburb.

Because DeFord was 11 at the time, he is being tried as a juvenile on eight counts of first-degree murder, eight counts of first-degree manslaughter and one count of felony arson. The maximum penalty is incarceration until his 25th birthday.

The court-appointed defense attorneys said DeFord was abused when he was younger, is borderline retarded and has the mental capacities of a 7-year-old. The boy has been kept at the Christie School, a center for disturbed youth, since shortly after the blaze.
Prosecutors argued in front of Washington County Circuit Judge Timothy Alexander that the boy was aware of what he was doing when he set the fire. There is no jury in the case.

Dressed in a green-striped shirt, jeans and loafer shoes, DeFord spent much of Wednesday's session doodling. He drew a simple picture of a devil-like figure with a pitchfork while Harrington presented her opening arguments.

During key testimony from Mexican immigrants who survived the blaze, DeFord alternated between doodling, fidgeting, whispering with defense attorney Charles Fryer and turning around to smile at an uncle who had attended the proceedings.
An entire family -- Jeremias Aguilar, 37; his wife, Virginia, 26; and their children, Karen, 10; Jacqueline, 8; Agustin, 7; and Patricia, 5, were killed in the fire.

Also killed were recently married Francisca Aguilar, 16, who had a 3-month-old baby, and her niece, Selena Chavez, also 3 months. About a dozen relatives of the victims attended the trial, many wearing earphones to listen to a translator.
Chief Deputy District Attorney Bob Herman said he was still unsure what punishment he would eventually ask for.
